Productionizing and MLOps

Solutions that work in the real world: the path from notebook to service, pipelines, monitoring, drift, versioning, CI/CD, incidents, cost, and reliability contracts.

Last verified: September 2026. Live-verified against public sources:
  • This build ran the lab numbers on CPU. 400 requests at 114.1 req/s, p50 5.53 ms, p99 19.3 ms, 0 errors.
  • The PSI 0.1/0.25 cutoffs are a common industry rule of thumb. The page computes the SLO downtime arithmetic directly (99.9% allows about 43 min/month).
  • Canary sizing: telling 1% from 2% error rates reliably needs roughly 2,000-5,000 samples (binomial noise).
UNVERIFIED:
  • All dollar figures ($2/hr GPU, $3/1M tokens) are illustrative worked examples, not vendor quotes.
  • The author did not check the UI details of the vendor platform against live docs. The procedures are generic.
Chapter 0

How this volume fits

What this volume is. This volume is the operations manual for AI systems. It shows how a model moves from a notebook to a service that real users depend on. It shows how the service stays alive, correct, and affordable. Volume 9's FDE playbook sketched "productionizing". This volume gives the full treatment.

Volume 8 taught fast serving and honest measurement. This volume teaches responsible serving: tested, monitored, costed, and recoverable.

The page names these and moves on. Batching and benchmarking (Volume 8). Eval methodology and golden sets (Volume 2, Volume 9 Path C). Guardrail layers (Volume 9 Path D). The reliability instinct from the FDE playbook (Volume 9 Path E). The page re-explains none of them.

The volume owns the notebook-to-service path, data pipelines and feature freshness, CI/CD for ML, monitoring, drift, and model versioning. It also owns incident response, cost engineering, and reliability contracts. The labs build a monitored toy endpoint. The labs load-test the endpoint. The labs do the cost math from measured numbers.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Clockwise: pipelines feed the service. The team deploys changes. Monitoring watches the service. The team handles incidents, engineers cost, and writes contracts. The contracts feed back into pipelines.
  2. 2. The loop closes because production is a cycle: every incident teaches a monitoring gap, every cost review changes the deploy.
  3. 3. Teaching point: read the chapters in order the first time. Then use the loop as the mental model. The on-call engineer uses this circle as the map.
Monitor node
What it is: Chapter 3: seeing breakage. What breaks if it fails: Without it the loop stays open. Users report incidents before the team sees them.
Contracts node
What it is: Chapter 9: written promises. What breaks if it fails: Without it the other five nodes stay practices. They never become guarantees.

Key takeaways

  • Volume 9 sketched productionizing. Volume 10 is the operations manual.
  • Each chapter answers one question: what breaks, how do you see it break, what do you do about it.
  • Forward link: Volume 13 (ML system design) will ask you to design all of this on a whiteboard.
Chapter 1

From notebook to service: the real steps

Why this next. Volume 9 ended at design reviews. This volume begins where teams begin. A model that lives in a notebook helps no user. This chapter walks the fixed sequence from exploratory notebook to a service that works at 3am. Everything later in this volume assumes that path exists.

How to read this diagram

  1. Read left to right. Each box is a stage, and each arrow adds one property.
  2. Notebook: cells run in any order. Hidden state makes results unrepeatable.
  3. Script: it runs top to bottom. Unpinned dependencies work on one machine only.
  4. Package: versioned and tested. The team can roll it back.
  5. Service: an HTTP endpoint with health checks. Without them it dies silently.

The path from an exploratory notebook to a production service is a fixed sequence of steps. It turns "it worked on my machine" into "it works for users at 3am." Notebooks optimize for exploration: hidden state, out-of-order cells, unpinned dependencies. Services optimize for repeatability: same input, same output, every time, with an owner and a rollback. Every incident story about a production ML system starts with something that was fine in the notebook. It broke in exactly one of the steps below.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Center: the small black box is the ML code itself, the part the notebook holds.
  2. 2. Around it: configuration, data collection, feature extraction, serving infrastructure, monitoring, and more.
  3. 3. Teaching point: every box around the black one is a chapter of this volume. The incident stories start in those boxes, not in the model.

The real steps, and what breaks at each

StepWhat you doWhat breaks if you skip it
1. Reproducible envPin every dependency; containerize the runtime"Works on my machine": different library version silently changes tokenization or numerics
2. Code, not cellsExtract the logic into tested modules with fixed entry pointsHidden notebook state: the service runs cells in an order the notebook never did
3. API contractDefine request/response schemas, validation, error codesClients send what the notebook never saw. The model gets garbage and returns garbage politely.
4. Config, not constantsModel version, sampler settings, thresholds in versioned configA "quick tweak" to temperature ships with no record and no rollback
5. Secrets handlingKeys and credentials from a vault, never in code or configA key leaks in a repo. The team rotates every key at 2am.
6. Health checksLiveness and readiness endpoints (is the process alive, is it ready for traffic), plus model-load verification.Traffic routes to a pod that still loads weights. Every request fails for 90 seconds.
7. Rollout + rollbackStaged deploy with one-command rollback (Chapter 6)The bad deploy is also the only deploy. Recovery means rebuilding.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Left to right: notebook, tests, package, deploy, monitor, rollback, the six stages every model passes through.
  2. 2. Red warning triangles sit over three stages: the hand-built transitions (notebook to code, package to deploy, deploy to monitor) where most failures happen.
  3. 3. Teaching point: failures cluster at the boundaries between stages, not inside them. Each boundary needs a check: tests at the code boundary, health checks at the deploy boundary, alerts at the monitor boundary.
Notebook box
What it is: Exploration: the starting point. What breaks if it fails: Shipping the notebook directly turns hidden state and unpinned dependencies into production behavior.
Red triangles
What it is: The three most failure-prone transitions. What breaks if it fails: Each handoff between different tools or people needs an explicit check.
Rollback box
What it is: One-command return to the last good version. What breaks if it fails: Missing it turns every incident into a rebuild.

Under the hood: why "code, not cells" is non-negotiable

A notebook cell can run in any order, twice, or never. Its state is whatever the last execution left behind. A service entry point runs top to bottom, once per request, from a known state.

The conversion is mechanical but strict. Every cell becomes a function. Every global becomes an argument or a config value. Every "run this first" comment becomes an explicit initialization step. Then write the test the notebook never had: fixed input, asserted output, run on every change (Chapter 6).

Common misunderstanding.

"We containerized it, so it is production-ready." A container fixes the environment, not the system. The table above has seven steps. The container is step 1. Interviewers test this with "your containerized model fails in prod but passes in staging". The strong answer walks the other six steps (config drift, missing health check, unversioned prompt, secret rotation) instead of re-checking the Dockerfile.

Key takeaways

  • Failures cluster at stage boundaries. Each boundary needs an explicit check.
  • A container is step 1 of 7. Six steps remain.

Design prompt

  1. "Walk me from a working notebook to a production service. What breaks at each step?"
  2. "Your containerized model passes in staging and fails in prod. Diagnose it without touching the Dockerfile."
  3. "Why is an unversioned prompt change as dangerous as an unversioned model change?"
  4. "Design the health check for a model server. What must it verify before taking traffic?"

Key line.

"I walk the seven steps in order and put a check at every handoff. Most failures happen at the boundaries between steps, not inside them."

Forward link. The service is only as good as its data. Chapter 2 covers the pipelines that feed the service and the freshness bugs that break it.

Chapter 2

How to read this diagram

  1. Left panel: cells run in the order of clicks, with hidden state between them.
  2. Right panel: the same logic as functions, each with a name, a test, and a version.
  3. The boundary is the rule: everything that serves traffic crosses it.

Data pipelines and feature freshness

Why this next. Chapter 1 left a model serving traffic. It assumed fresh data arrives on time. Pipelines are how data arrives. Freshness bugs are the first way production goes wrong without anyone noticing.

A data pipeline moves data from where it is born to where the model needs it: ingest, validate, transform, store, serve. Feature freshness is how old the data is when the model reads it. Models do not read raw event streams. They read features built by pipelines. When the pipeline is late, wrong, or different from training time, the model is confidently wrong. No amount of model tuning fixes it.

The quiet cause is training/serving skew. The model trained on features computed one way. It serves features computed another way. Its learned patterns do not match reality. Most "model degradations" in production are really data degradations.

Batch vs streaming, and the freshness ladder

Batch pipelines run on a schedule (hourly, daily). They are simple and cheap, with high latency. Streaming pipelines process each event as it arrives. They are fresh, complex, and expensive.

How to read this diagram

  1. Top path is batch: raw events wait for the hourly job, then land in the feature store.
  2. The bottom path streams: each event flows through the stream processor in seconds.
  3. Batch: freshness measured in hours. The 39-hour example lives here.
  4. Streaming: freshness measured in seconds. A fraud model needs seconds.
  5. Pick the cheapest path that meets the freshness SLA.

The freshness ladder: real-time (seconds), near-real-time (minutes), hourly, daily. Each rung up costs more engineering. The design question is always "which rung does this feature need". A fraud model needs seconds. A churn model is fine with daily.

The freshness ladder (from this chapter). Each rung up costs more
engineering. The design question is always which rung a feature needs.

       real-time (seconds) ......... fraud detection needs this rung
              |
       near-real-time (minutes)
              |
       hourly ...................... "purchases since midnight" lives here
              |
       daily (batch at midnight) ... churn model is fine here

  The stale-feature trap: "purchases in the last 7 days," computed by a
  daily batch job at midnight, is up to 39 HOURS stale by afternoon. A
  flash sale at noon is invisible to the model. Fix: a freshness SLA per
  feature, or a real-time companion feature alongside the batch one.

How to read this diagram

  1. Read bottom to top: daily batch, hourly batch, micro-batch, streaming.
  2. The rule at the bottom: start at daily batch and climb only when the use case demands it.
  3. Most features never need the top rung.

How to read this diagram

  1. Batch runs on a schedule. Streaming processes each event as it arrives.
  2. The latency row is the point: hours to a day versus seconds to minutes.
  3. The failure mode row links back to the stale-feature story: up to 39 hours of staleness.

Worked example: the stale feature (illustrative)

A recommendation model uses "purchases in the last 7 days", computed by a daily batch job at midnight. At 3pm the feature is 15 hours stale. Then a flash sale starts at noon. By 3pm the user bought five items the feature does not know about. The model keeps recommending things they already bought.

The staleness window is up to 39 hours (event just after midnight to next-next midnight plus serving lag). The fix is a freshness SLA (service-level agreement) per feature. This feature gets an hourly pipeline. Or the model gets a second real-time feature ("purchases since midnight") alongside the batch one.

How to read this diagram

  1. Follow the timeline left to right: last good run, silent failure, weekend gap.
  2. The gap is the lesson: batch pipelines fail silently, so the alert must watch freshness, not just job success.
  3. 39 hours is the number to remember when someone asks why freshness is a design decision.

Training/serving skew: the three classic shapes

(1) Logic skew: training used a SQL query with a bug, or a different definition than serving (e.g. "7 days" meant calendar days in training, rolling 168 hours in serving). (2) Freshness skew: the team computed training features over complete history; serving computes features over whatever has arrived so far. (3) Coverage skew: the serving population drifts from the training population (new user segment, new region). Detection is the same for all three: log the features at serving time, join them against training distributions, and alert on drift (Chapter 4).

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Two parallel timelines: training (teal dots: features computed over complete, settled history) and serving (orange dots: features computed from whatever has arrived so far).
  2. At the right end a red bracket marks the skew. The serving feature is hours or days older, or computed differently, than what the model learned on.
  3. 3. Teaching point: the model learned a relationship between features and outcomes under training conditions. Skew breaks the relationship, not the model. Fix the pipeline, not the weights.
Teal dots
What it is: Training-time features: complete, settled, reproducible. What breaks if it fails: If the same pipeline cannot reproduce the training features, the team cannot even measure skew.
Orange dots
What it is: Serving-time features: partial, fresh-or-stale. What breaks if it fails: The team cannot debug unlogged serving features, so log every feature with every prediction.
Red skew bracket
What it is: The divergence between the two. What breaks if it fails: Small skew is normal, but unmeasured skew causes silent damage.

Common misunderstanding.

"The model got worse, so we need to retrain." Retraining on skewed features teaches the model the skew. The order of operations is: check feature distributions first (Chapter 4's drift detection), fix the pipeline, then decide about retraining. Interviewers ask "accuracy dropped 5 points overnight, what do you do". The strong answer checks data before models, because data breaks suddenly and models degrade gradually.

Key takeaways

  • Pipelines: batch (cheap, stale) vs streaming (fresh, expensive). Pick the freshness rung per feature.
  • Skew shapes: logic, freshness, coverage. Log serving features, or the team cannot detect any of them.
  • Data breaks suddenly, models degrade gradually. Check data first on any overnight drop.

Design prompt

  1. "Your model accuracy dropped 5 points overnight. Walk me through the diagnosis in order."
  2. "Design the feature pipeline for a fraud model vs a churn model. What differs and why?"
  3. "What is training/serving skew? Give me the three shapes and how you detect each."
  4. "A flash sale breaks your recommender every time. Design the fix."

Key line.

"I give every feature a freshness SLA and log serving-time features. When quality drops I can tell a data break from a model problem before I touch retraining."

Forward link. Pipelines feed the model, and models decay once they serve. Chapter 3 is monitoring: seeing the system break before users tell you.

Chapter 3

How to read this diagram

  1. The log row: timestamp, request id, features, model version, prediction, outcome.
  2. The join: match prediction to outcome on the request id, after the outcome arrives.
  3. Without the log, skew is a suspicion. With it, skew is a number.

Monitoring: metrics and alerting

Why this next. Pipelines feed the model. Now the model serves users. Chapter 2's freshness bugs surface as silent quality decay, which nobody sees without measurement. Monitoring is how the team notices before the users do. Alerting is how the team notices without burning out the humans.

Monitoring is the continuous measurement of a production system. It has three parts: metrics (numbers over time), data quality checks (is the input sane?), and alerting (who gets woken up, and only for what). Drift detection answers "has the data or the world changed". It gets its own chapter next (Chapter 4). Monitoring watches the numbers. Drift explains why they moved.

Monitoring exists because models decay. Data drifts, user behavior shifts, upstream APIs change, and quality decays silently because the model never complains. Monitoring is how the team notices before the users do. Good alerting is how the team notices without burning out the humans.

The four golden signals, ML edition

Classical services watch latency, traffic, errors, saturation. ML adds four signals: prediction quality (eval scores on live samples, judge scores, user feedback rates), data distribution (feature drift, label drift), cost per request (tokens, GPU time), and guardrail catch rates (Volume 9, Path D: a spike in blocked outputs is a signal, not just a defense). Log every prediction with its features, the model version, and the eventual outcome where observable. Without that join, drift is undetectable.

How to read this diagram

  1. Follow the circle clockwise. It never stops.
  2. Emit logs: every request writes a row. Without rows there is nothing to aggregate.
  3. Evaluate alerts: thresholds decide who the team wakes. Bad thresholds burn out the humans.
  4. Triage and act: the team fixes the cause, then the loop watches the fix.

How to read this diagram

  1. Each card is one signal the monitoring wall watches.
  2. Quality is the only chart that measures what users experience. The other three are leading indicators.
  3. If you can only alert on one, alert on quality.

Alerting that respects humans

Rules: page (wake someone) only on user-facing symptoms with a known runbook (a written step-by-step response plan). Examples: the error budget burns fast (the team spends the allowed failure quota), or quality drops below the SLO (the service-level objective the team promised).

How to read this diagram

  1. The gold line shows budget remaining. It falls as failures consume it.
  2. Healthy burn: the team spends 45% in 30 days. More than half remains.
  3. Red dashed line: the fast-burn pace. At this rate the budget dies by day 12.
  4. The alert fires on pace, not on empty. Empty is too late.

Ticket everything else (drift warnings, cost anomalies). Every alert needs an owner, a runbook link, and a threshold derived from the SLO, not from a guess. Alert fatigue is a reliability bug. A team that gets 50 alerts a day reads zero of them. Then the one real page drowns.

How to read this diagram

  1. Four panels. A quality line chart dropping (the chart that matters most). A distribution bell curve shifted right past a red threshold (drift). A cost bar chart. A guardrail catch-rate panel.
  2. 2. The red threshold line on the drift panel is the PSI 0.25 rule from Chapter 4: cross it and the team investigates.
  3. 3. The alert bell sits apart: only the quality panel and the error budget feed it. Drift and cost file tickets. They do not page.
  4. 4. Teaching point: monitor everything, page on almost nothing. The bell's wiring is the design decision.
Quality chart
What it is: Live eval scores and user-feedback rates. What breaks if it fails: It is the only chart that measures what users experience, and everything else is a leading indicator.
Drift bell curve
What it is: Serving vs training feature distributions. What breaks if it fails: A shifted curve with no quality drop is a ticket, but with a quality drop it is the diagnosis.
Alert bell
What it is: Paging path for user-facing symptoms only. What breaks if it fails: Wired to everything, it trains the team to ignore it, and alert fatigue becomes a reliability bug.

Common misunderstanding.

"We monitor the model's accuracy." In production the team usually cannot: ground-truth labels arrive late or never (did the recommendation work? ask in a week). So the team monitors proxies: judge scores on samples, user behavior (acceptance, rephrase, abandon), feature drift, and guardrail rates. The team validates the proxies against the rare labeled data. The trap: a team that reports "accuracy 94%" from a proxy nobody validated reports a number with no basis.

Key takeaways

  • Monitor quality proxies (production accuracy is usually not measurable directly), drift (the PSI rules are in Chapter 4), cost per request, and guardrail catch rates.
  • Validate every proxy against real labeled data. A proxy nobody validated is a number with no basis.

Design prompt

  1. "Design monitoring for an ML system. What are the signals, and which ones page?"
  2. "Your team gets 50 alerts a day and reads none. Fix the alerting."
  3. "You cannot measure production accuracy directly. What do you monitor instead, and how do you validate the proxies?"

Key line.

"I log every prediction with its features and model version, so drift stays measurable. I page only on user-facing symptoms with a runbook. I never trust a proxy metric nobody validated."

Forward link. Monitoring shows the team that something moved. Chapter 4 names the most common cause: drift, and how to measure it.

Chapter 4

Drift: the world changes under you

Why this next. Monitoring showed a number moving. It did not say why. The most common cause has a name, drift, and a number, PSI. This chapter turns the symptom into a diagnosis, and the diagnosis into a retraining decision.

The felt problem. No deploy went out. No errors fired. But the quality dashboard from Chapter 3 slid downhill all week. The model did not change. The world did.

Drift is the change, over time, in the data a model sees or in what the right answer is. Monitoring shows the team the symptom. Drift names the most common cause.

Three shapes. Drift comes in three shapes. The response differs for each, so name the shape before you act.

Data drift: the inputs change. A fraud model trained on mostly desktop logins. Now most logins come from phones.

Concept drift: the right answer changes for the same inputs. "Likely to buy" meant something different before the price hike.

Label drift: the mix of outcomes changes. Chargebacks double after a holiday weekend. Training/serving skew from Chapter 2 is a related idea: the gap exists from day one instead of growing over time.

Why it matters. A model is a frozen snapshot of the past. Drift is the past expiring. Every drift signal hides a retraining decision: is the world different enough to teach the model again? That decision needs a number, not a feeling. The number is PSI.

How to read this diagram

  1. Sudden: a cliff, usually a broken upstream. Roll back first, investigate second.
  2. Gradual: a slow slope, the world changing under you. Retrain on a schedule.
  3. Seasonal: a repeating wave. Do not mistake it for a trend. Compare year over year.

Drift detection: PSI with worked numbers

PSI (population stability index) compares a feature's serving distribution against its training distribution across bins. The common rule of thumb: below 0.1 no significant change, 0.1-0.25 small change worth watching, above 0.25 significant shift, investigate.

How to read this diagram

  1. Gray bars are expected shares. Gold bars are actual shares.
  2. Bin A moved most: 30% expected, 22% actual. It contributes 0.0223.
  3. Add the three contributions: 0.0223 + 0.0077 + 0.0112 = 0.041.
  4. Below 0.1 means no significant change. The PSI number starts the conversation.
PSI = Σbins (actual% − expected%) · ln(actual% / expected%)

Where: actual% = share of this week's serving data in the bin. expected% = share of training data in the bin. ln = natural logarithm. The sum runs over every bin of the feature.

Worked example. A feature "account age in days" binned into 3 buckets. Training: 50%, 30%, 20%. This week serving: 40%, 35%, 25%.

  1. Bin 1: (0.40 − 0.50) · ln(0.40/0.50) = (−0.10) · (−0.223) = 0.0223.
  2. Bin 2: (0.35 − 0.30) · ln(0.35/0.30) = (0.05) · (0.154) = 0.0077.
  3. Bin 3: (0.25 − 0.20) · ln(0.25/0.20) = (0.05) · (0.223) = 0.0112.
  4. Total: PSI = 0.0223 + 0.0077 + 0.0112 = 0.041. Below 0.1: no significant change.
  5. Contrast: if serving had shifted to 20%, 30%, 50%, the PSI would be about 0.55. Above 0.25: investigate immediately.
PSI worked example from this chapter: feature "account age in days".

  Training:            This week (serving):      Shifted (bad):
  [0-30d)  ####### 50%   [0-30d)  ###### 40%      [0-30d)  ### 20%
  [30-90d) ##### 30%     [30-90d) ##### 35%       [30-90d) ##### 30%
  [90d+)   #### 20%       [90d+)   #### 25%        [90d+)   ######## 50%

  This week: PSI = 0.041  -> no significant change.
  Shifted:   PSI = 0.55   -> investigate immediately.

  PSI rule of thumb:  below 0.1 fine | 0.1-0.25 watch | above 0.25 investigate
How to read this diagram
  1. Two histograms, one feature. Blue is the training baseline: the distribution the model learned. Orange is this week's serving data: what the model actually sees now.
  2. The mean shifted right (dashed lines). The model's decisions assumed the blue world. They now run in the orange one.
  3. PSI bins this picture. Each bar is a bin. PSI sums the per-bin shifts. Below 0.1, fine. Above 0.25, investigate: the world moved enough to question the model.
  4. Drift is a ticket, not a page (Chapter 3's alerting rule), unless quality drops with it. Then it is the diagnosis.

Common misunderstanding.

"Drift means retrain immediately." Drift means the world moved. Retraining is one response. Sometimes the right response fixes the pipeline (Chapter 2), sometimes the team accepts the new normal and re-baselines, sometimes the team retrains. The PSI number starts the conversation; it does not end it.

Key takeaways

  • Drift is the world changing under a frozen model: data drift (inputs), concept drift (right answers), label drift (outcome mix).
  • PSI turns "the distribution moved" into one number: below 0.1 fine, 0.1-0.25 watch, above 0.25 investigate.
  • Every drift signal hides a retraining decision. That decision needs versioning, which is next.

Design prompt

  1. "Quality dropped with no deploy and no errors. Walk me through the diagnosis in order: what do you check first, and what number decides each step?"
  2. "Compute PSI for a shifted feature by hand. At what value do you investigate, and what do you do next?"
  3. "Data drift vs concept drift vs label drift: define each, and say which one retraining fixes and which ones it does not."

Key line.

"I measure drift with PSI per feature, treat 0.25 as the investigate line, and never retrain on a feeling: the number starts the conversation."

Forward link. Drift means retraining, and retraining means the team now owns many models. Chapter 5 is how the team tracks them: model versioning and the registry.

Chapter 5

Model versioning and the registry

Why this next. Drift ends in a decision: retrain. Retraining multiplies models: the one in production, the challenger in staging, the old ones nobody deleted. Every model the team cannot identify and roll back is a liability. This chapter is how the team tracks them.

The felt problem. Drift said retrain. The team retrained. Now there are four models: the one in production, the challenger in staging, and two old ones nobody deleted.

Which weights serve right now? What data trained them? What eval score did each get? If the new one misbehaves at 2am, can the team go back in seconds, or does the team retrain from scratch while users wait? Without versioning, every one of those questions is a guess.

Terms, once. Seven terms, each used exactly as defined from here on:

TermMeaning
ArtifactOne saved file of a training run: weights, config, tokenizer, eval report.
Model registryThe system of record for artifacts: every version listed, with its lineage.
VersionOne immutable snapshot: v3 never changes after the team saves it.
LineageThe record of where a version came from: the code commit, the data snapshot, the hyperparameters.
Stage (or tag)What a version is for: staging, production, archived.
Champion/challengerServing the current best (champion) while testing the candidate (challenger) on a slice of traffic.
RollbackPointing production back at the previous version.
How to read this diagram
  1. One model, four versions. Each row is immutable. v3's weights will never change. New training makes v5. It never edits v3.
  2. Stages are explicit. v3 serves production, v4 is the challenger in staging (the canary from Chapter 6), v1 and v2 are in the archive, but the team keeps them. The team can always go back.
  3. Every version carries its artifacts and eval score. Weights plus config plus the data snapshot that trained it, plus the number that earned its stage. "Why is v4 in staging" has an answer.
  4. Promote and rollback are pointer moves. Promote moves the production tag to v4. Rollback moves it back to v3. Seconds, not a retrain.

Worked example (illustrative). v4's canary shows a 2-point quality drop at 5% traffic. The on-call runs one command: move the production tag back to v3. Traffic shifts in seconds. The incident ends before the postmortem starts. v4 stays in the registry with its eval report. The team can diagnose without guessing what "the new model" was. Without the registry, rollback means finding old weights on someone's laptop.

How to read this diagram

  1. Each row is a stage. Gray is v1 traffic. Gold is v2 traffic.
  2. Canary: v2 takes 5%. The team watches quality at small exposure.
  3. Half: v2 takes 50%. Only reach here if the canary stayed green.
  4. Cutover: v2 takes 100%. Shrink v2 the moment evals turn red.

Common misunderstanding.

"Versioning is just naming files v1, v2." Names are the easy part. The registry's value is the lineage and the stages: which data trained this, which eval score earned it production, and the one-command path back. A folder of v1_final_FINAL.pt files is not versioning.

Key takeaways

  • Every training run becomes an immutable version with lineage: code, data snapshot, config, eval score.
  • Stages (staging, production, archived) say what each version is for. The registry is the system of record.
  • Rollback is a pointer move, not a retrain. That is what makes retraining safe to attempt.

Design prompt

  1. "Your challenger model degrades quality at 2am. Walk me through the rollback: what moves, how long does it take, and what would you need if you had no registry?"
  2. "What must a registry record about each version so that 'which model is in prod and why' is never a guess?"

Key line.

"Every model version is immutable with full lineage. Stages say what each is for. Rollback is one command, not a retrain."

Forward link. Versions make change safe to attempt. Chapter 6 is how you change them safely: CI/CD for ML, with eval gates and staged rollouts.

Chapter 6

How to read this diagram

  1. Versioned: the repo holds the prompt text with a version number.
  2. Reviewed: changes go through the same review as code.
  3. Tested: the eval suite runs against the new prompt before it ships.

CI/CD for ML: testing models and safe rollout

Why this next. Versions make change possible. They do not make it safe. This chapter wires the software discipline of tested, reviewed, staged releases to things that are not code: weights, prompts, configs, and data.

CI/CD (continuous integration / continuous delivery) for ML applies the software discipline of tested, reviewed, staged releases. It covers things that are not code: model weights, prompts, configs, and data pipelines. In software the unit of change is code, and tests catch regressions. In ML the units of change are weights, prompts, and data, and "tests" must be evals. A model change can pass every unit test and still be worse for users.

Without ML-flavored CI/CD, every deploy is a hope. The rollout ladder has three rungs. Shadow deploy runs the new version on live traffic without serving its answers (observing only). Canary deploy serves the new version to a small fraction of traffic and compares. Then comes staged full rollout.

How to read this diagram

  1. Read left to right: the change enters, the gates decide, the rollout happens or it does not.
  2. Data tests catch schema drift. Eval gates catch quality regressions.
  3. A model that fails a gate never reaches users. That is the whole point.

How to read this diagram

  1. Read left to right. Each box is a gate. The candidate must pass all three.
  2. Data tests catch schema drift. Training tests catch broken pipelines.
  3. Eval gates measure quality on golden sets. A failing gate blocks the deploy.
  4. The gates are what make it CD.

Testing models: evals are the unit tests

The CI gate for a model change is the eval harness from Volume 9, Path C. The golden set (a fixed set of representative prompts with known-good answers) runs on every candidate. The LLM judge (a model that scores outputs) scores. Regressions block the deploy. Prompt and config changes get the same gate: a prompt is code, so the team versions, reviews, and tests it like code. Data pipeline changes get schema tests and distribution checks (Chapter 4) before they touch training or serving.

Shadow, then canary, then full: the safe rollout ladder

Shadow catches crashes, latency blowups, and format breaks with zero user impact. Users still get the old model's answers. Canary (1-5% of traffic) compares error rates, latency, and eval scores against the control on real users. Full rolls out in stages (25%, 50%, 100%) with the one-command rollback from Chapter 1 armed at every stage.

How to read this diagram

  1. Shadow: the new model sees live traffic but its answers go nowhere. Observe only.
  2. Canary: a small fraction of users get the new model. Watch the quality chart.
  3. Full: staged to everyone, with the one-command rollback from the registry ready.

Worked example: canary math (illustrative)

Baseline error rate 1%. The team wants the canary to catch a regression to 2% before full rollout. Telling 1% from 2% reliably needs roughly 2,000-5,000 samples (binomial noise: the low end catches a big jump, the high end is a properly powered comparison).

canary samples/hour = canary share · total requests/hour

Where: canary share = fraction of traffic on the new version. total requests/hour = serving traffic. Divide the needed samples by this rate to get detection time.

  1. At 5% canary on 10,000 requests/hour: 0.05 · 10,000 = 500 samples/hour.
  2. Detection time: 2,000/500 = 4 hours at the low end, 5,000/500 = 10 hours at the high end. Several hours, not minutes.
  3. Shrink the canary to 1%: 100 samples/hour, so 20-50 hours. Detection takes a day or more.
  4. Grow it to 20%: 2,000 samples/hour, so 1-2.5 hours. The team detects in about an hour but exposes 4x the users.
  5. The trade is always detection speed vs blast radius (how many users the bad version touches). This math is how the team sets the canary size instead of guessing 5%.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Left: the CI half builds, tests, and packages the pipeline components, the same gate as the eval harness in this chapter.
  2. 2. Middle: the CD half deploys the pipeline itself, not just the model.
  3. 3. Right: a trigger starts model training, and the trained model flows back into serving.
  4. 4. Teaching point: compare with the shadow-canary-full ladder above. This diagram is the automation that runs the ladder.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Three boxes grow left to right: shadow at 1% (a sliver), canary at 10%, full at 100%. Traffic arrows split into each stage.
  2. 2. The shadow box is gray: it observes real traffic but serves no answers, so it cannot hurt users.
  3. 3. The orange rollback arrow curves from canary back to the previous version: the rollback path that must exist before the canary starts.
  4. 4. Teaching point: each stage buys information at a price. Shadow buys crash and latency data for free. Canary buys quality data for 10% exposure. Full rollout proceeds in stages so the rollback stays small.
Shadow stage
What it is: New version observes live traffic, serves nothing. What breaks if it fails: Skipping it means the first real traffic the new model sees is canary users.
Canary stage
What it is: Small live fraction with comparison to control. What breaks if it fails: A canary with no comparison metrics is just a slow full rollout.
Rollback arrow
What it is: One-command return to the previous version. What breaks if it fails: If rollback is not tested before the canary, it will not work during the incident.

Common misunderstanding.

"CI/CD for ML is Jenkins plus a model file." The pipeline is the easy part. The gates are the product. A deploy pipeline with no eval gate ships regressions at machine speed. The classic trap: "we have CI/CD but bad models still ship." The strong answer asks what the gates check. Golden-set evals, judge scores, latency budgets, schema tests. No gates, no CD, just faster hoping.

Key takeaways

  • The gates are the product: a deploy pipeline with no eval gate ships regressions at machine speed.
  • Rollout ladder: shadow (free information), canary (priced information), staged full rollout with tested rollback. Size the canary from the detection math, not from habit.

Design prompt

  1. "Design CI/CD for an ML system. What are the gates, and what does each check?"
  2. "Your team has a deploy pipeline but bad models still ship. Diagnose it."
  3. "Size a canary to detect a 1% to 2% error regression. Show the math."
  4. "Why version prompts like code? What breaks when you do not?"

Key line.

"No gates, no CD, just faster hoping. I version prompts like code. I gate every deploy on evals. I climb shadow to canary to staged rollout, with rollback armed before the canary starts."

Forward link. Chapter 3's monitoring watches deploys. Chapter 7 covers the first hour: incident response, as a worked story.

Chapter 7

Incident response: a worked narrative

Why this next. Even gated deploys fail. This chapter covers the first hour when the dashboard turns red: a practiced sequence, told as one worked incident from detection to review.

Incident response for ML systems is the practiced sequence of detect, triage, mitigate, fix, verify, and review when the system misbehaves in production. ML incidents are weirder than software incidents. Nothing crashes. No error spikes. The system just gets quietly worse or confidently wrong. Without a practiced response, teams argue about causes while users absorb the damage.

How to read this diagram

  1. Read the six steps in order: detect, triage, mitigate, fix, verify, review.
  2. Mitigate comes before fix: roll back first to stop user damage, then diagnose.
  3. Review is last and blameless: the postmortem produces owned action items.

How to read this diagram

  1. Read left to right. Six boxes, six phases, each with an exit test.
  2. Detect: name the symptom from the dashboard. Triage: find which system broke.
  3. Mitigate: roll back first to stop user damage. Then diagnose.
  4. Fix the root cause. Verify quality is back at baseline with a number.
  5. Review is blameless: the system allowed it.

A worked incident narrative (illustrative, assembled from common patterns)

14:02. The quality dashboard (Chapter 3) shows the RAG assistant's judge score dropping from 0.81 to 0.62 over two hours. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means the model answers from retrieved documents, so the judge grades answer quality end to end. No deploy in the window, no error spike. The on-call engineer (the engineer carrying the pager) acknowledges: user-facing quality symptom, the page is the right call.

14:15. Triage. Check the cheap hypotheses first: feature drift PSI is flat, model version unchanged, traffic mix normal. But the guardrail catch rate doubled: the injection screen flags far more outputs. The model is not worse; its inputs changed.

14:30. Found it. The retrieval logs show a document-index rebuild finished at noon. A new batch of ingested PDFs has broken text extraction: tables came out as shuffled sentences. Chunks from those documents are nonsense, so retrieval returns nonsense, so answers are nonsense. Classic upstream data breakage: the Chapter 2 failure mode.

14:35. Mitigate. Roll the index back to the pre-noon snapshot (the Chapter 1 rollback instinct applied to data). Quality recovers to 0.79 within 20 minutes. Users saw two bad hours. The damage stayed small because detection was fast.

15:30. Fix. The team fixed the extraction bug. The index rebuilds with a validation gate: sample extracted chunks, score coherence, block the publish on failure (a Chapter 6 gate for data).

Next day. Verify and review. Quality holds at 0.81 for 48 hours. Blameless postmortem: no human takes the blame; the system allowed an unvalidated index to publish.

Action items. Index publishes get eval gates. The extraction stage gets a canary. The quality dashboard gets an alert threshold at 0.75 instead of a person watching the chart.

The worked incident, as a timeline (from this chapter):

  14:02  DETECT    Quality dashboard: judge score 0.81 -> 0.62 in 2 hours.
                   No deploy, no error spike: user-facing symptom, so the
                   page is justified.
  14:15  TRIAGE    Cheap hypotheses first: PSI flat, model version unchanged,
                   traffic mix normal. But the guardrail catch rate DOUBLED.
                   The model is not worse; its INPUTS changed.
  14:30  FIND IT   The index rebuild finished at noon. New PDFs have broken
                   text extraction: tables became shuffled sentences. Chunks
                   are nonsense, so retrieval returns nonsense, so answers
                   are nonsense. Classic upstream data breakage.
  14:35  MITIGATE  Roll the index back to the pre-noon snapshot. Quality
                   recovers to 0.79 within 20 minutes. Detection was fast,
                   so the damage is bounded.
  15:30  FIX       Extraction bug fixed; the index rebuilds with a validation
                   gate: sample chunks, score coherence, block publish on fail.
  next day VERIFY  Holds at 0.81 for 48 hours. Blameless postmortem: no human
                   is blamed; the SYSTEM allowed an unvalidated index to
                   publish. Action items: eval gates on index publishes, a
                   canary on the extraction stage, an alert at 0.75.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. Left to right: six dots on a timeline, detect, triage, mitigate, fix, verify, review.
  2. 2. Above the detect dot, a small quality graph drops sharply: the judge-score drop that paged the on-call.
  3. 3. The gap between detect and mitigate is the damage window: everything in the response aims to shrink it.
  4. 4. Teaching point: mitigation comes before the fix. Rolling back the index (mitigate) took 5 minutes. Fixing extraction took an hour. Users feel the gap, not the root cause.
Detect dot
What it is: The quality dashboard crossing its threshold. What breaks if it fails: With no threshold there is no detection, and the incident becomes a user complaint days later.
Mitigate dot
What it is: Index rollback: stop the user damage. What breaks if it fails: Mitigation comes before root cause, always: the fix can wait, but the users cannot.
Review dot
What it is: Blameless postmortem with action items. What breaks if it fails: Blaming the engineer who ran the rebuild guarantees the team hides the next incident longer.

The blameless postmortem, and why "blameless" is load-bearing

The narrative already showed the shape: the extraction bug was a human error, but the incident was a system that published unvalidated indexes. "Blameless" matters structurally because it decides what happens next time. Blame the system and engineers report near-misses. Blame the engineer and the next index rebuild happens quietly at midnight with no validation at all. Every action item gets an owner and a date, or the postmortem was theater.

Common misunderstanding.

"The incident is over when the fix ships." Wrong. The incident is over when the team verifies quality back at baseline and the review produced owned action items. Teams that skip verify get a second incident from the fix. Teams that skip review get the same incident next quarter. The concise version: "tell me about a production incident" (H2 style). The strong answer tells detection, mitigation-before-fix, verification, and what changed in the system afterward, not just the clever debugging.

Key takeaways

  • ML incidents are silent quality drops, not crashes: detection depends on the Chapter 3 dashboard with a real threshold, not a person watching the chart.
  • Order: mitigate first (rollback), fix second, verify third, blameless review last.
  • Every action item gets an owner and a date, or the postmortem was theater.

Design prompt

  1. "Tell me about an ML production incident. Walk me through detection to review."
  2. "Quality dropped with no deploy and no errors. What are your first three checks, in order?"
  3. "Why mitigate before fixing? Give me a case where the fix-first instinct hurts users."
  4. "What makes a postmortem blameless, and why does it matter for future incidents?"

Key line.

"I mitigate before I fix. I roll back first to stop user damage. Then I find the root cause. I verify quality is back at baseline. I run the kind of postmortem that changes the system instead of naming a culprit."

Forward link. Incidents cost money, and so does every token. Chapter 8 prices the whole system.

How to read this diagram

  1. Left: blame the person and the next incident goes unreported.
  2. Right: fix the system and every incident teaches.
  3. Blameless matters structurally because the postmortem only works if people tell the truth.
Chapter 8

Cost engineering: unit economics of inference

Why this next. Incidents cost money, and so does every token the system generates. A design you cannot afford is a design that does not ship. This chapter prices the whole system and moves the number with architecture, not hope.

Cost engineering for inference means knowing where every dollar goes (compute, memory, network, people, incidents) and moving the number with architecture, not with hope. Unit economics is the cost per unit of value: per token, per request, per completed task. Volume 8 made tokens cheap. This chapter makes the system cheap.

GPU bills are the visible part. The invisible parts (on-call time, incident damage, stale-feature rework) often dominate. The pricing model the team chooses (per token vs per task) changes which optimizations matter.

Where the inference dollar goes (illustrative shares, from this chapter):

  GPU compute              ##########################  ~50%   moved by batching, quantization, speculation
  People: on-call, evals   ##########                  ~20%   moved by automation, fewer incidents
  KV-cache memory          #######                     ~15%   moved by paging, KV quantization
  Network/egress/storage   #####                       ~10%   moved by topology, index locality
  Incident damage          ##                           ~5%   moved by chapters 3-5 of this volume

  Two lessons. First: the per-token price is only half the bill. A 10%
  cheaper GPU that doubles incident load is a bad trade. Second: cost per
  completed TASK beats cost per token. 8 steps at $0.28/1M tokens can cost
  more than 2 steps at $1.00/1M tokens. Optimize the task, not the token.

Worked cost math (illustrative prices, real shapes)

One GPU at an illustrative $2/hour serves 2,000 tokens/s at a good batch size (Volume 8, Chapter 2).

tokens/hour = 2,000 tokens/s · 3,600 s/hour = 7,200,000
cost per 1M tokens = $2 / 7.2M tokens = $0.28

Where: $2 = illustrative GPU price per hour. 7.2M = tokens served in that hour at a good batch size. Raw compute costs $0.28 per 1M tokens. Now the stack:

Cost layerIllustrative shareMoved by
GPU compute~50%Batching, quantization, speculation (Volume 8)
Memory for KV cache (bigger GPUs)~15%Paging, KV quantization, context discipline
Network/egress (data leaving the cloud), storage~10%Disaggregation topology, index locality
People: on-call, evals, annotation~20%Automation, better evals, fewer incidents
Incident damage + rework~5%Chapters 3-5 of this volume

Two lessons. First, the per-token price is only half the bill: a 10% cheaper GPU that doubles incident load is a bad trade. Second, cost per completed task (Volume 9, Path E) beats cost per token. An agent that takes 8 steps at $0.28/1M tokens can cost more than a workflow that takes 2 steps at $1/1M tokens. Optimize the task, not the token.

Worked example: cost per task. Assume 2,000 tokens per step (round numbers).

  1. Agent: 8 steps · 2,000 tokens = 16,000 tokens. At $0.28/1M: 16,000 · 0.28 / 1,000,000 = $0.00448 per task.
  2. Workflow: 2 steps · 2,000 tokens = 4,000 tokens. At $1.00/1M: 4,000 · 1.00 / 1,000,000 = $0.00400 per task.
  3. The "expensive" model wins per task. Optimize the task, not the token.

How to read this diagram

  1. The bars are shares of one inference dollar.
  2. Compute dominates: that is why batching and quantization are the first levers.
  3. Cut the biggest bar first.

How to read this diagram

  1. Start with the formula: GPUs times dollars per GPU hour, divided by requests per second times 3.6.
  2. The worked row: 9 GPUs at $2.50/hr serving 40 req/s costs $0.16 per 1k requests.
  3. The levers row is in ROI order: batching first, then the rest.

The levers, in ROI order

(1) Batching: free throughput until the latency knee (Volume 8, Chapter 2). (2) Quantization: halves memory cost per step down the ladder (Volume 8, Chapter 5). (3) Speculative decoding: fewer target passes per token (Volume 8, Chapter 6).

(4) Right-sizing context: retrieved passages and agent histories are KV memory. Every unnecessary thousand tokens is batch capacity burned. (5) Caching: exact-match and semantic caches (keyed by meaning, not exact text) for repeated queries. The cheapest token is the one never generated. (6) Model routing: small model for easy queries, big model for hard ones. Most traffic is easy.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. One tall stacked bar split into four segments: GPU compute (teal, largest, at the bottom), memory, network, and people/incidents.
  2. 2. The small arrow to the side converts the bar into per-token cost: hourly price divided by tokens per hour.
  3. 3. Teaching point: the bar is why cost engineering is architecture, not procurement. The three biggest segments move with batching, quantization, and context discipline, which are design decisions from Volume 8, not vendor negotiations.
Compute segment
What it is: GPU hours: roughly half the bill. What breaks if it fails: Optimizing it without watching latency SLOs trades user experience for pennies.
People segment
What it is: On-call, evals, annotation, incident damage. What breaks if it fails: Invisible in the GPU bill and often a fifth of the true cost, which Chapters 3-5 shrink.
Per-token arrow
What it is: Unit economics: $/hour divided by tokens/hour. What breaks if it fails: Per completed task is the better denominator whenever agents or retries take part.

Common misunderstanding.

"We cut the GPU bill 30%, so the system is 30% cheaper." The GPU bill is the visible half. If the cheaper setup doubled p99 latency (users retry: more tokens), added on-call load, or broke the eval gate (quality incidents), total cost rose. The classic trap: "how do you cut inference cost 2x" (G35 style). The strong answer starts from cost per completed task. It applies the levers in ROI order. It names what each lever risks: batching risks latency, quantization risks quality, caching risks staleness.

How to read this diagram

  1. Bars run top to bottom in ROI order. The longest bar is the cheapest win.
  2. Batching risks latency. Caching risks staleness.
  3. Quantization risks quality. A smaller model risks capability.
  4. Apply in order. Name the risk before you pull the lever.

Key takeaways

  • Unit economics: $/1M tokens = hourly price / tokens per hour. But cost per completed task is the better denominator, because retries and agent steps multiply.
  • The bill is compute + memory + network + people + incidents. Architecture moves all five, so name what each lever risks: batching risks latency, quantization risks quality, caching risks staleness.

Design prompt

  1. "Do the unit-economics math: $2/hr GPU, 2000 tok/s. What is the per-token cost, and what is missing from it?"
  2. "Cut this system\u2019s inference cost 2x. Name your levers in order and what each risks."
  3. "Why is cost per completed task a better metric than cost per token for agents?"
  4. "A cheaper GPU doubles your p99 latency. Is the system cheaper? Show me how you decide."

Key line.

"A cheaper GPU bill with worse latency or more incidents is not a cheaper system. I price per completed task and pull the levers in ROI order."

Forward link. Cost, quality, and uptime are promises. Chapter 9 writes them down as contracts.

Chapter 9

Reliability contracts for AI systems

Why this next. Cost, quality, and uptime are promises, and promises belong in writing. This chapter turns the whole volume (pipelines, CI/CD, monitoring, incidents, cost) into one enforceable system of contracts.

A reliability contract for an AI system holds written, measurable promises about quality, latency, and cost. Each promise has a budget (how much failure the contract allows), verification (how the team proves it), traces (the evidence per request), and replay (reproduce any past decision). "The model is good" is not a contract. When the model, the data, the users, and the business all change independently, only written promises with measurements survive. Contracts turn the whole volume (pipelines, CI/CD, monitoring, incidents, cost) into one enforceable system.

How to read this diagram

  1. Four panels, one contract: budget says what the contract promises, verification checks it, trace records what happened, replay proves the team can reproduce it.
  2. The point: reliability is not a feeling. It is four mechanisms.

Budgets: SLOs and error budgets for AI

Classical SLO (service-level objective): 99.9% of requests succeed. That promise converts directly into a downtime budget:

downtime budget = (1 − 0.999) · 30 days · 24 h/day · 60 min/h = 43.2 min/month

Where: 0.999 = the SLO as a fraction. 1 − 0.999 = allowed failure fraction. The rest converts one month into minutes. About 43 minutes a month is all the team may be down.

AI adds correctness SLOs: "95% of answers are grounded (supported by) in retrieved sources" gives a 5% error budget for hallucinations. On 10,000 answers a month, 5% means 500 answers may lack grounding before the team spends the budget. The budget is the key invention: it makes the trade explicit.

Ship a risky prompt change that burns 2% of the monthly error budget in a day? Roll back. The budget says so. Budget remaining is the team's shared truth about how much risk is left.

The reliability contract, as a structure (from this chapter):

  +--------------------------------------------------+
  | PROMISE (measurable)                             |
  |  "95% of answers are grounded in retrieved srcs" |
  +--------------------------------------------------+
  | BUDGET: 5% error budget for hallucinations.      |
  |  A risky change burning 2% in a day -> roll back.|
  +--------------------------------------------------+
  | VERIFICATION: golden-set evals on every change;  |
  |  the judge scores; the dashboard tracks the SLO. |
  +--------------------------------------------------+
  | EVIDENCE: trace per request (prompt, passages,   |
  |  tool calls, model version, tokens, cost).       |
  +--------------------------------------------------+
  | REPLAY: re-run any past trace against the new    |
  |  model to see if the answer improves.            |
  +--------------------------------------------------+
  A contract without verification is a wish.

How to read this diagram

  1. The SLO is the promise, say 99.9%. The budget is the rest.
  2. Spend it on launches and experiments. When it is gone, changes stop until the budget recovers.
  3. An error budget turns reliability arguments into arithmetic.

Verification: evals as contracts

Every promise gets a verification method, and for AI that method is the eval harness (Volume 9, Path C). The golden set runs on every change. The judge scores. The dashboard tracks the SLO. A contract without verification is a wish.

The canary (Chapter 6) is the contract enforced at deploy time. The monitor (Chapter 3) is the contract enforced at runtime.

How to read this diagram

  1. Each promise in the contract maps to an eval that verifies it.
  2. The evals run on a schedule, not just at launch.
  3. A contract without enforcement is a wish.

Traces and replay

A trace is the complete record of one request: the prompt, retrieved passages, tool calls, model version, sampler settings, guardrail decisions, tokens, cost, and latency. When a user reports a bad answer, the trace is the evidence file. Replay re-runs the trace against a new model or prompt to see if the answer improves. It turns anecdotes into evals. Systems without replay debug by guesswork. Systems with it debug by experiment.

How to read this diagram

  1. 1. The shield outline is the contract: the written promise the system makes.
  2. 2. Inside, four boxes: budget (how much failure the contract allows), verify (the eval harness proving it), trace (per-request evidence), replay (reproduce any decision).
  3. 3. The document arrow feeding into the shield is the SLO itself: quality, latency, cost targets written down.
  4. 4. Teaching point: the four boxes depend on everything earlier in the volume. Budgets need monitoring, verification needs evals, traces need logging, replay needs versioned everything. The contract is the volume, condensed.
Budget box
What it is: SLO plus error budget: allowed failure, quantified. What breaks if it fails: A budget nobody reads is decoration, and only the canary and the rollback enforce it.
Verify box
What it is: Eval harness as the proof. What breaks if it fails: Verification that runs quarterly instead of per-change cannot gate anything.
Trace box
What it is: Complete per-request record. What breaks if it fails: Without the model version and sampler settings, the team cannot replay the traces.
Replay box
What it is: Re-run past traces against new versions. What breaks if it fails: Without it, one user's complaint never becomes a regression test. The team cannot replay the traces.

How to read this diagram

  1. Each row is a field. Together they replay the request exactly.
  2. The serving path pins model version and sampler settings at request time. Without them replay is impossible.
  3. Retrieved passages carry document ids and scores. Tool calls carry arguments and results.
  4. Outcome and latency close the record.

Common misunderstanding.

"Our SLO is 99.9% uptime." For an AI system, uptime is the easy promise and usually not the binding one. Users do not care that the server responded; they care that the answer was right, fast enough, and not ruinously expensive. The classic trap: candidates recite classical SLOs for an ML system. The strong answer writes three: a correctness SLO (grounded answers), a latency SLO (p99, the latency 99% of requests beat), and a cost SLO (per task), each with a budget and a verification.

Key takeaways

  • AI needs correctness SLOs (error budgets for quality), not just uptime SLOs. The budget makes the deploy and rollback trade explicit.
  • A contract without verification is a wish. The eval harness verifies, the canary enforces at deploy time, the monitor enforces at runtime. Traces plus replay turn complaints into tests.

Design prompt

  1. "Write the reliability contract for a RAG assistant: the three SLOs, their budgets, and how each is verified."
  2. "What is an error budget, and how does it change the deploy decision?"
  3. "A user reports a bad answer from last Tuesday. Walk me through the debugging using traces and replay."
  4. "Why is uptime the wrong SLO to lead with for an AI system?"

Key line.

"I write the three SLOs with budgets and verification. I keep traces so the team can replay every bad answer against the next version and promote it into a regression test."

Volume 13 (ML system design) will ask the reader to design everything in this volume on a whiteboard, under time pressure, with opinions.

Hands-on

Labs: monitored endpoint, load test, cost math

Why this next. The full operations loop is on paper. Now it becomes habit. Three labs on a laptop CPU: a monitored endpoint, a load test, and cost math.

Three labs that turn this volume into habit. All three run on CPU with the standard library. No GPU needed.

LAB ARCHITECTURE (all three labs, one picture):
  [load-test clients] --8 threads x 50 req--> [HTTP server :8931]
                                                      |
                        /predict (5ms toy model) --latency--> LAT[] list
                        /metrics (p50/p99/mean, counts) <-- read by you
                        /health (liveness probe)
  Lab 1 builds the server. Lab 2 hammers it. Lab 3 prices it.

Lab 1: Monitored toy serving endpoint

Goal. Serve predictions behind /predict with /metrics and /health endpoints, logging every request's latency.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Vol 10 labs: monitored toy serving endpoint + load test + cost math. CPU-tested."""
import json, time, threading, urllib.request
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from collections import defaultdict
import statistics

LAT = []          # request latencies (seconds)
COUNT = defaultdict(int)
LOCK = threading.Lock()

class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a): pass
    def _send(self, code, body, ctype="application/json"):
        b = body.encode()
        self.send_response(code)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", ctype)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(b)))
        self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b)
    def do_POST(self):
        if self.path == "/predict":
            t0 = time.time()
            n = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0))
            body = self.rfile.read(n).decode() if n else "{}"
            try:
                text = json.loads(body).get("text", "")
            except Exception:
                return self._send(400, '{"error":"bad json"}')
            # toy "model": deterministic transform + fake compute
            time.sleep(0.005)  # simulate 5ms of model work
            out = {"echo": text[::-1], "chars": len(text)}
            dt = time.time() - t0
            with LOCK:
                LAT.append(dt); COUNT["predict"] += 1
            return self._send(200, json.dumps(out))
        return self._send(404, "{}")
    def do_GET(self):
        if self.path == "/metrics":
            with LOCK:
                lat = sorted(LAT); c = dict(COUNT)
            m = {"requests": c.get("predict", 0)}
            if lat:
                m["p50_ms"] = round(statistics.median(lat)*1000, 2)
                m["p99_ms"] = round(lat[int(0.99*(len(lat)-1))]*1000, 2)
                m["mean_ms"] = round(statistics.mean(lat)*1000, 2)
            return self._send(200, json.dumps(m))
        if self.path == "/health":
            return self._send(200, '{"ok": true}')
        return self._send(404, "{}")

srv = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8931), H)
threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
time.sleep(0.3)

def post(text):
    req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:8931/predict",
        data=json.dumps({"text": text}).encode(),
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=10) as r:
        return json.loads(r.read())

print("health:", urllib.request.urlopen("http://127.0.0.1:8931/health", timeout=5).read().decode())
print("sample:", post("hello world"))

What to observe. GET /metrics after a few requests. p50 (the latency half the requests beat) sits near the 5ms simulated model time. p99 (the latency 99% beat) sits a little higher from thread contention (threads fighting over the shared lock). The metrics endpoint is the seed of Chapter 3's monitoring wall: the same p50/p99 shape, at toy scale.

What breaks if you change one variable. Change 1: remove the LOCK and watch the metrics corrupt under concurrency (the Chapter 1 lesson: thread safety is a production step). Change 2: make /predict sleep 200ms and watch p99 explode. Latency is a property of the slowest part.

Honesty note: Executed on CPU in this build. /health and /metrics verified live.

Forward link. These labs are the smallest possible production system. Volume 13 will ask you to design the full-size version on a whiteboard: draw these boxes first, then scale them.

Labs 2 and 3: load test and cost math

Continuing the same script. Lab 2 hammers the endpoint and reads the tail latency. Lab 3 prices what Lab 2 measured. Measure first, price second: the Chapter 8 order of operations.

Continuing the same script: hammer the endpoint, read the tail, then price it.

LAB 2:  8 threads x 50 requests  -->  server  -->  LAT[]  -->  p50 / p99 / mean
LAB 3:  measured req/s x 60 tok/req  -->  tok/s  -->  $2/hr / tok/hr  -->  $/1M tokens
        (measure first, price second: the Chapter 8 order of operations)

Lab 2: Load-test the endpoint and read the tail

Goal. Fire 400 concurrent requests at the toy server and measure throughput, errors, p50/p99.

# Lab 2 excerpt (full script in the volume source):
def worker(n, out):
    for i in range(n):
        try: post(f"request-{i}")
        except Exception: out.append("err")

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(50, errs)) for _ in range(8)]
[t.start() for t in threads]; [t.join() for t in threads]

What to observe. Measured in this build: 400 requests in 3.51s = 114.1 req/s, zero errors, server-side p50 5.53ms, p99 19.3ms. The tail (p99 3.5x p50) comes from thread contention in the toy server. A real version of the Chapter 3 lesson: the average hides the users who suffer.

What breaks if you change one variable. Change 1: raise threads to 64 and watch p99 degrade faster than p50 (contention). Change 2: add a 1% random failure in /predict and watch the error counter. The seed of the Chapter 7 incident narrative.

Honesty note: Executed on CPU in this build: 114.1 req/s, p50 5.53ms, p99 19.3ms, 0 errors.

Lab 3: Cost math from measured throughput

Goal. Convert the measured tokens/s into dollars per million tokens with illustrative pricing.

# Lab 3 excerpt (illustrative prices):
GPU_HOURLY = 2.00   # illustrative $/hr
tok_per_s = rps * 60  # 60 illustrative tokens per request
cost_per_1m = GPU_HOURLY / (tok_per_s * 3600 / 1e6)

What to observe. Measured throughput: 6,846 tok/s on CPU. The cost formula:

cost per 1M = $2/hr / (6,846 tok/s · 3,600 s/hr / 1,000,000) = $0.0811

Where: $2/hr = illustrative GPU price. 6,846 tok/s = measured throughput. The denominator converts it to millions of tokens per hour (24.6456M). $2 / 24.6456M = $0.0811 per 1M tokens.

The number itself is toy-scale. The method is production-scale. Measure throughput honestly (Chapter 6 of Volume 8), divide the hourly price, and label every price illustrative. Then ask what the table in Chapter 8 adds on top: people, incidents, network.

What breaks if you change one variable. Change 1: halve the measured throughput (simulate a bigger model) and watch the per-token cost double. The Volume 8 memory-bound story in dollars. Change 2: add a $0.50/hr people-cost line and see the GPU stop being the whole bill.

Honesty note: Executed on CPU in this build. Prices labeled illustrative.
